title: A Symplectic Proof of the Quantum Singleton Bound
summary: We present a symplectic linear-algebraic proof of the Quantum Singleton Bound for stabiliser quantum error-correcting codes together with a Lean4 formalisation of the linear-algebraic argument. The proof is formulated in the language of finite-dimensional symplectic vector spaces modelling Pauli operators and relies on distance-based erasure correctability and the cleaning lemma. Using a dimension-counting argument within the symplectic stabiliser framework, we derive the bound \( k + 2(d - 1) \le n \) for any [[n, k, d]] stabiliser code. This approach isolates the algebraic structure underlying the bound and avoids the heavier analytic machinery that appears in entropy-based proofs, while remaining well-suited to formal verification.

AI.tldr: Formalized symplectic linear-algebraic proof of Quantum Singleton Bound for stabilizer codes using Lean4, deriving k + 2(d-1) ≤ n via dimension counting in symplectic vector spaces.
AI.motivation: To provide a clean, algebraic proof of the Quantum Singleton Bound for stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes that avoids heavy analytic machinery and is suitable for formal verification.
AI.method: Uses finite-dimensional symplectic vector spaces to model Pauli operators, applies distance-based erasure correctability and the cleaning lemma, and employs dimension-counting arguments within the symplectic stabilizer framework.
AI.result: Successfully derives the bound k + 2(d - 1) ≤ n for any [[n, k, d]] stabilizer code, with the proof formalized in Lean4.
AI.conclusion: The symplectic linear-algebraic approach isolates the algebraic structure underlying the Quantum Singleton Bound, provides a formalizable proof, and avoids entropy-based analytic machinery while maintaining mathematical rigor.

title: Quantum Simulations for Extreme Ultraviolet Photolithography
summary: Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is the state-of-the-art process in semiconductor fabrication, yet its spatial resolution is fundamentally limited by the ``blur'' originating from absorption of photons at 92 eV, which induce physical and chemical changes in the photoresist via excited state processes and electron cascades. Accurate modeling of these phenomena requires precise ab initio data for high-energy decay channels, specifically photoabsorption and photoelectron emission. These are computationally difficult for classical methods due to prohibitive scaling in simulating electron dynamics, or due to the inability to resolve the ionization continuum in an efficient manner. In this work, we present quantum simulation algorithms to compute these key observables. First, we introduce a coherent time-domain spectroscopy algorithm optimized to resolve the photoabsorption cross-section at the 92 eV operating frequency. Second, we develop a first-quantized plane-wave simulation to compute the photoelectron kinetic energy spectrum, utilizing real-time dynamics and energy windowing to treat bound and delocalized scattering states on equal footing. Additionally, we provide logical resource estimation for a model photoresist monomer, 4-iodo-2-methylphenol (IMePh), and demonstrate that 92 eV absorption sensitivity can be resolved using roughly $200$ logical qubits and $10^{9}$ total non-Clifford gates per circuit with approximately $10^3$ shots for the smallest instance. The more sophisticated photoemission algorithm that models the continuum explicitly, incurs gate costs of $\geq 10^{13}$ total non-Clifford gates per circuit, $10^4$ shots, and requires a few thousand logical qubits. These results establish high-fidelity quantum simulations as a key component to parameterize the multi-scale macroscopic models required to overcome the electron blur bottleneck in semiconductor miniaturization.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithms for EUV lithography modeling: time-domain spectroscopy for photoabsorption and plane-wave simulation for photoelectron spectra, with resource estimates for 4-iodo-2-methylphenol photoresist monomer.
AI.motivation: EUV lithography resolution is limited by photon absorption blur at 92 eV; accurate modeling requires precise ab initio data for high-energy decay channels (photoabsorption and photoelectron emission), which are computationally difficult for classical methods due to scaling issues with electron dynamics and ionization continuum resolution.
AI.method: Two quantum simulation algorithms: 1) coherent time-domain spectroscopy optimized for 92 eV photoabsorption cross-section resolution; 2) first-quantized plane-wave simulation for photoelectron kinetic energy spectrum using real-time dynamics and energy windowing to treat bound and scattering states equally.
AI.result: Resource estimation for model photoresist monomer (4-iodo-2-methylphenol): photoabsorption requires ~200 logical qubits, 10^9 non-Clifford gates per circuit, ~10^3 shots; photoemission requires ≥10^13 non-Clifford gates per circuit, 10^4 shots, few thousand logical qubits.
AI.conclusion: High-fidelity quantum simulations can parameterize multi-scale macroscopic models to overcome electron blur bottleneck in semiconductor miniaturization, establishing quantum computing as key component for EUV lithography advancement.

title: Proof of a finite threshold for the union-find decoder
summary: Fast decoders that achieve strong error suppression are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) from both practical and theoretical perspectives. The union-find (UF) decoder for the surface code is widely regarded as a promising candidate, offering almost-linear time complexity and favorable empirical error suppression supported by numerical evidence. However, the lack of a rigorous threshold theorem has left open whether the UF decoder can achieve fault tolerance beyond the error models and parameter regimes tested in numerical simulations. Here, we provide a rigorous proof of a finite threshold for the UF decoder on the surface code under the circuit-level local stochastic error model. To this end, we develop a refined error-clustering framework that extends techniques previously used to analyze cellular-automaton and renormalization-group decoders, by showing that error clusters can be separated by substantially larger buffers, thereby enabling analytical control over the behavior of the UF decoder. Using this guarantee, we further prove a quasi-polylogarithmic upper bound on the average runtime of a parallel UF decoder in terms of the code size. We also show that this framework yields a finite threshold for the greedy decoder, a simpler decoder with lower complexity but weaker empirical error suppression. These results provide a solid theoretical foundation for the practical use of UF-based decoders in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computers, while offering a unified framework for studying fault tolerance across these practical decoders.

AI.tldr: Rigorous proof of finite threshold for union-find decoder on surface code under circuit-level local stochastic error model, with quasi-polylogarithmic runtime bound and extension to greedy decoder.
AI.motivation: Fast decoders with strong error suppression are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. While union-find decoder shows promise with almost-linear time complexity and good empirical performance, it lacks rigorous theoretical foundation regarding fault tolerance beyond tested regimes.
AI.method: Developed refined error-clustering framework extending techniques from cellular-automaton and renormalization-group decoders. Showed error clusters can be separated by substantially larger buffers, enabling analytical control over UF decoder behavior.
AI.result: Proved finite threshold for UF decoder on surface code under circuit-level local stochastic error model. Established quasi-polylogarithmic upper bound on average runtime of parallel UF decoder in terms of code size. Framework also yields finite threshold for greedy decoder.
AI.conclusion: Provides solid theoretical foundation for practical use of UF-based decoders in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Offers unified framework for studying fault tolerance across practical decoders, bridging gap between empirical performance and rigorous theoretical guarantees.

title: Construction of a Neural Network with Temperature-Dependent Recall Patterns
summary: We present a simple model that recalls two different patterns depending on the temperature. To realize a change in recall pattern due to temperature change, we embed two patterns to different graphs: the first pattern into a fully connected graph and the second pattern into a sparse graph. Because a fully connected graph is more resistant to thermal fluctuations than a sparse graph, we can realize a change in recall pattern by tuning relative weights of the two patterns properly. We demonstrate by equilibrium Monte-Carlo simulations that such a temperature-dependent change in recall patterns does occur in our model. Simulation results strongly indicate that the system undergoes a first-order phase transition when the change in recall patterns occurs. It is also demonstrated by annealing simulations that the system fails to recall the pattern embedded in the sparse graph at low temperatures if the free-energy barrier is too high to overcome within the given simulation timescale.

AI.tldr: A neural network model that recalls different patterns based on temperature by embedding patterns in graphs with different connectivity (fully connected vs. sparse), showing temperature-dependent recall patterns via first-order phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To create a simple model that exhibits temperature-dependent pattern recall, leveraging the different thermal stability properties of fully connected versus sparse graph embeddings.
AI.method: Embed two patterns into different graph structures: first pattern into a fully connected graph (more thermally stable), second pattern into a sparse graph. Use equilibrium Monte-Carlo simulations to demonstrate temperature-dependent recall pattern changes, and annealing simulations to show recall failure when free-energy barriers are too high.
AI.result: The model successfully shows temperature-dependent pattern recall changes, with evidence of first-order phase transitions during pattern switching. Annealing simulations reveal that the sparse-graph pattern fails to recall at low temperatures when free-energy barriers exceed simulation timescales.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-dependent pattern recall can be achieved by embedding patterns in graphs with different connectivity, with fully connected graphs providing thermal stability and sparse graphs enabling temperature-sensitive switching via first-order phase transitions.

title: Time Crystals as Passively Protected Oscillating Qubits
summary: Protecting information against decoherence in open quantum systems remains a central challenge for quantum computing. In particular, passive error correction schemes have so far been limited to static memories rather than dynamical qubits. We demonstrate that a driven-dissipative bosonic system can encode a persistently oscillating qubit within a noiseless subsystem, realized explicitly in the Bose-Hubbard dimer (BHD). The strong parity symmetry of the model leads to degenerate stationary states. This symmetry is further broken into non-stationary states in the thermodynamic limit, which exhibit persistent oscillations. As the driving force increases, the Liouvillian spectrum of these states features a phase transition. Above the transition point, the non-stationary state encodes quantum information, preserving it in a noiseless subsystem. In addition to global loss that affects both bosonic modes identically, we further add global dephasing and show that the oscillating qubit is preserved. Finally, in order to gain additional physical insight, we study the effect of phase perturbation to both modes and observe that likewise they are passively protected, returning approximately to their initial configurations. These results establish dissipative time-crystalline dynamics as a mechanism for passive protection of dynamical quantum information, enabling autonomously stabilized oscillating qubits.

AI.tldr: A driven-dissipative bosonic system can encode persistently oscillating qubits within noiseless subsystems, enabling passive protection of dynamical quantum information through dissipative time-crystalline dynamics.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of protecting quantum information against decoherence in open quantum systems, particularly for dynamical qubits rather than just static memories, and to develop passive error correction schemes that don't require active intervention.
AI.method: Using a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard dimer (BHD) with strong parity symmetry that leads to degenerate stationary states. The symmetry is broken into non-stationary states in the thermodynamic limit, creating persistent oscillations. The system is analyzed through Liouvillian spectrum phase transitions and tested against various noise types including global loss, global dephasing, and phase perturbations.
AI.result: The system exhibits a phase transition where above a critical driving force, non-stationary states encode quantum information in a noiseless subsystem. The oscillating qubit is preserved against global loss, global dephasing, and phase perturbations, with the system returning approximately to initial configurations after perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative time-crystalline dynamics provide a mechanism for passive protection of dynamical quantum information, enabling autonomously stabilized oscillating qubits that are robust against various types of noise and decoherence.

title: Quantum algorithm for simulating resonant inelastic X-ray scattering in battery materials
summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is the workhorse experimental technique for probing the structural degradation of higher-capacity cathode materials. However, the interpretation of experimental spectra is challenging due to the lack of accurate simulations. In this work, we propose a quantum algorithm for simulating the RIXS spectrum of molecular clusters hypothesized to form in Li-excess cathodes. The algorithm uses quantum phase estimation to sample the spectrum from a state encoding the scattering transition amplitudes of the cluster valence excitations. We prepare this state in the quantum computer using a block-encoding of the dipole operator and quantum signal processing to implement the Green's function propagator over intermediate core-excited states. To showcase the algorithm, we use a model cluster proposed in recent experimental works consisting of an oxygen dimer bonded to a manganese atom. Using the PennyLane software platform, we report resource estimation for simulating RIXS spectra for chemically motivated active spaces of increasing sizes. For a classically challenging active space with 20 orbitals, the algorithm requires $2.0 \times 10^{10}$ Toffoli gates and $414$ logical qubits.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for simulating resonant inelastic X-ray scattering spectra of molecular clusters in Li-excess cathodes using quantum phase estimation and quantum signal processing.
AI.motivation: RIXS is crucial for studying cathode material degradation, but interpreting experimental spectra is difficult due to lack of accurate simulations. Current classical methods struggle with complex molecular clusters.
AI.method: Quantum algorithm using quantum phase estimation to sample RIXS spectrum from scattering transition amplitudes. Employs block-encoding of dipole operator and quantum signal processing to implement Green's function propagator over intermediate core-excited states.
AI.result: Resource estimation for simulating RIXS spectra shows that for a classically challenging active space with 20 orbitals, the algorithm requires 2.0×10¹⁰ Toffoli gates and 414 logical qubits. Demonstrated on model cluster of oxygen dimer bonded to manganese atom.
AI.conclusion: Proposed quantum algorithm enables accurate simulation of RIXS spectra for complex molecular clusters in cathode materials, addressing current limitations in interpreting experimental data for battery research.

title: Pulse-level control for quantum resource preparation
summary: Minimizing the time required for quantum state preparation is crucial to mitigate decoherence and enable practical quantum algorithms on near-term hardware. In this work, we introduce a technique for quantum state preparation in transmon-qubit systems using optimized electromagnetic pulse sequences rather than discrete quantum gates. By directly targeting quantum correlations instead of specific target states, we identify minimal-time pulse protocols that optimize relevant entanglement resources, such as concurrence and the three-tangle for two and three qubit systems, respectively. For the figures of merit considered, this approach successfully achieves maximal entanglement in each case: Bell, GHZ and W like states. Beyond state preparation, the resource-oriented nature of the approach leads to a reduced effective expressivity of the control scheme, a feature that represents an advantage in algorithmic settings where excessive control freedom is known to hinder performance.

AI.tldr: Optimized electromagnetic pulse sequences for quantum state preparation in transmon-qubit systems, targeting quantum correlations rather than specific states to achieve minimal-time protocols and maximal entanglement.
AI.motivation: Minimizing quantum state preparation time is crucial to mitigate decoherence and enable practical quantum algorithms on near-term hardware, as faster preparation reduces exposure to environmental noise and errors.
AI.method: Introduces a technique using optimized electromagnetic pulse sequences instead of discrete quantum gates, directly targeting quantum correlations (entanglement resources like concurrence and three-tangle) rather than specific target states to identify minimal-time pulse protocols.
AI.result: Successfully achieves maximal entanglement for Bell, GHZ, and W-like states in two and three qubit systems, with the resource-oriented approach leading to reduced effective expressivity of the control scheme.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables faster state preparation while providing an advantage in algorithmic settings where excessive control freedom hinders performance, representing a practical method for near-term quantum hardware.

title: Entanglement Barriers from Computational Complexity: Matrix-Product-State Approach to Satisfiability
summary: We approach the 3-SAT satisfiability problem with the quantum-inspired method of imaginary time propagation (ITP) applied to matrix product states (MPS) on a classical computer. This ansatz is fundamentally limited by a quantum entanglement barrier that emerges in imaginary time, reflecting the exponential hardness expected for this NP-complete problem. Strikingly, we argue based on careful analysis of the structure imprinted onto the MPS by the 3-SAT instances that this barrier arises from classical computational complexity. To reveal this connection, we elucidate with stochastic models the specific relationship between the classical hardness of the $\sharp$P $\supseteq$ NP-complete counting problem $\sharp$3-SAT and the entanglement properties of the quantum state. Our findings illuminate the limitations of this quantum-inspired approach and demonstrate how purely classical computational complexity can manifest in quantum entanglement. Furthermore, we present estimates of the non-stabilizerness required by the protocol, finding a similar resource barrier. Specifically, the necessary amount of non-Clifford operations scales superlinearly in system size, thus implying extensive resource requirements of ITP on different architectures such as Clifford circuits or gate-based quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes limitations of quantum-inspired imaginary time propagation (ITP) on matrix product states (MPS) for solving 3-SAT, showing entanglement barriers reflect classical computational complexity and requiring extensive non-Clifford resources.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limitations of quantum-inspired approaches (specifically imaginary time propagation on matrix product states) for solving NP-complete problems like 3-SAT, and to investigate how classical computational complexity manifests in quantum entanglement properties.
AI.method: Apply imaginary time propagation (ITP) to matrix product states (MPS) on classical computers to solve 3-SAT instances. Analyze entanglement properties of resulting MPS and use stochastic models to connect classical computational complexity (#3-SAT counting problem) with quantum entanglement barriers.
AI.result: The method encounters a quantum entanglement barrier in imaginary time that reflects the exponential hardness of 3-SAT. This barrier arises from classical computational complexity, specifically the #P ⊇ NP-complete counting problem #3-SAT. The protocol requires superlinear scaling of non-Clifford operations with system size, indicating extensive resource requirements.
AI.conclusion: Classical computational complexity fundamentally limits quantum-inspired approaches like ITP on MPS for solving NP-complete problems. The entanglement barrier observed is not merely a quantum phenomenon but reflects underlying classical hardness. Additionally, the approach requires extensive non-Clifford resources, making it impractical for different computational architectures.

title: Quantifying Effective Heterodyne Detection Efficiency with SI-Traceable Standards
summary: Accurate calibration of coherent optical receivers is essential for reliable performance assessment in coherent communications, precision and quantum sensing, and continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD), where the effective detection efficiency directly impacts channel parameter estimation. We present a methodology traceable to the International System of Units (SI) to determine the effective heterodyne detection efficiency of balanced receivers using shot-noise-referenced measurements. The protocol relies on two observables acquired with an electrical spectrum analyzer: the heterodyne beat-note power and the local oscillator shot-noise variance, with explicit treatment of the analyzer's equivalent noise bandwidth (ENBW). The photon flux in the signal path is referenced to SI units via calibrated radiometric standards. We first validate the protocol on a free-space receiver, demonstrating consistency with an independently constructed optical loss chain across a wide range of signal powers and under controlled, calibrated attenuation. Extending the same estimator to a fiber-coupled, polarization-maintaining balanced receiver confirms that the protocol is robust for practical coherent-receiver architectures and intermediate frequencies in the MHz range. These results establish a traceable, uncertainty-bounded framework for real-time receiver calibration, providing a practical route for CV-QKD and other coherent optical systems.

AI.tldr: Traceable SI calibration method for coherent optical receivers using shot-noise-referenced measurements to determine effective heterodyne detection efficiency.
AI.motivation: Accurate calibration of coherent optical receivers is essential for reliable performance assessment in coherent communications, precision/quantum sensing, and CV-QKD, where effective detection efficiency directly impacts channel parameter estimation.
AI.method: SI-traceable methodology using shot-noise-referenced measurements with two observables from electrical spectrum analyzer: heterodyne beat-note power and local oscillator shot-noise variance, with explicit treatment of analyzer's equivalent noise bandwidth. Photon flux in signal path referenced to SI units via calibrated radiometric standards.
AI.result: Protocol validated on free-space receiver showing consistency with independently constructed optical loss chain across wide signal power range under controlled attenuation. Extended to fiber-coupled, polarization-maintaining balanced receiver confirms robustness for practical coherent-receiver architectures at MHz intermediate frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Establishes traceable, uncertainty-bounded framework for real-time receiver calibration, providing practical route for CV-QKD and other coherent optical systems.

title: No change in Hilbert space fundamentalism
summary:
Hilbert space fundamentalism (HSF) states that everything about the physical world is encoded in the Hamiltonian operator and the state vector (as a unit vector, not a wavefunction, which requires additional specification of a configuration space, a position basis, or the position observables). That all structures needed to describe reality, including subsystems, space, fields, emerge from these.
  I show that HSF can't account for our observations that the physical world changes in time.

AI.tldr: HSF cannot explain temporal change in physical observations despite claiming all reality emerges from Hamiltonian and state vector.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that Hilbert Space Fundamentalism (HSF) fails to account for observed temporal changes in the physical world, despite its claim that all physical structures emerge from the Hamiltonian operator and state vector.
AI.method: The author presents a logical/philosophical analysis showing that HSF's framework (Hamiltonian operator + state vector) cannot accommodate our observations of temporal change in the physical world.
AI.result: HSF is shown to be inadequate for explaining temporal change, as the Hamiltonian operator and state vector alone cannot account for our observations of a changing physical world.
AI.conclusion: Hilbert Space Fundamentalism fails as a complete physical theory because it cannot explain the fundamental observation that the physical world changes in time.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Complex Systems
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) is rapidly transitioning from theoretical promise to practical relevance across data-intensive scientific domains. In this Review, we provide a structured overview of recent advances that bridge foundational quantum learning principles with real-world applications. We survey foundational QML paradigms, including variational quantum algorithms, quantum kernel methods, and neural-network quantum states, with emphasis on their applicability to complex quantum systems. We examine neural-network quantum states as expressive variational models for correlated matter, non-equilibrium dynamics, and open quantum systems, and discuss fundamental challenges associated with training and sampling. Recent advances in quantum-enhanced sampling and diagnostics of learning dynamics, including information-theoretic tools, are reviewed as mechanisms for improving scalability and trainability. The Review further highlights application-driven QML frameworks in drug discovery, cancer biology, and agro-climate modeling, where data complexity and constraints motivate hybrid quantum-classical approaches. We conclude with a discussion of federated quantum machine learning as a route to distributed, privacy-preserving quantum intelligence. Overall, this Review presents a unified perspective on the opportunities and limitations of QML for complex systems.

AI.tldr: Review paper surveying recent advances in quantum machine learning (QML), covering foundational paradigms, neural-network quantum states, quantum-enhanced sampling, and real-world applications in scientific domains, with discussion of federated QML for distributed privacy-preserving quantum intelligence.
AI.motivation: QML is transitioning from theoretical promise to practical relevance in data-intensive scientific domains. The paper aims to provide a structured overview bridging foundational quantum learning principles with real-world applications, addressing the need to understand both opportunities and limitations of QML for complex systems.
AI.method: Review methodology: structured overview surveying foundational QML paradigms (variational quantum algorithms, quantum kernel methods, neural-network quantum states), examining neural-network quantum states for correlated matter and quantum systems, reviewing quantum-enhanced sampling and learning diagnostics, highlighting application-driven frameworks, and discussing federated quantum machine learning approaches.
AI.result: The review presents a unified perspective on QML advances, covering: 1) Foundational paradigms with emphasis on applicability to complex quantum systems, 2) Neural-network quantum states as expressive variational models for various quantum phenomena, 3) Recent advances in quantum-enhanced sampling and learning diagnostics, 4) Application-driven frameworks in drug discovery, cancer biology, and agro-climate modeling, 5) Federated QML as a route to distributed, privacy-preserving quantum intelligence.
AI.conclusion: QML offers significant opportunities for complex systems but faces fundamental challenges in training and sampling. The review provides a unified perspective on both opportunities and limitations, highlighting the transition from theoretical promise to practical relevance and the potential of hybrid quantum-classical approaches and federated quantum machine learning for distributed, privacy-preserving applications.

title: Measurement-Guided State Refinement for Shallow Feedback-Based Quantum Optimization Algorithm
summary: Limited circuit depth remains a central constraint for quantum optimization in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime, where shallow unitary dynamics may fail to sufficiently concentrate probability on low-energy configurations. We introduce Measurement-Guided Initialization (MGI), an iterative strategy that uses measurement outcomes from previous executions to update the initialization of subsequent runs. The method extracts single-qubit marginal probabilities from dominant measurement outcomes and prepares a biased product-state initialization, allowing information obtained during optimization to be reused without introducing classical parameter optimization. We implement this approach in the context of the Feedback-Based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) and evaluate its performance on weighted MaxCut instances. Numerical results show that measurement-guided initialization improves the performance of shallow-depth circuits and enables iterative refinement toward high-quality solutions while preserving the non-variational structure of the algorithm. These results indicate that measurement statistics can be exploited to improve shallow quantum optimization protocols compatible with NISQ devices.

AI.tldr: MGI (Measurement-Guided Initialization) improves shallow quantum optimization by using measurement outcomes to bias initial states, enhancing performance on NISQ devices without classical parameter optimization.
AI.motivation: Limited circuit depth in NISQ devices restricts quantum optimization performance, as shallow circuits may not sufficiently concentrate probability on low-energy configurations. There's a need to improve shallow quantum optimization protocols without introducing classical parameter optimization overhead.
AI.method: MGI is an iterative strategy that extracts single-qubit marginal probabilities from dominant measurement outcomes and prepares a biased product-state initialization for subsequent runs. This allows information from previous executions to be reused. The approach is implemented within the FALQON (Feedback-Based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization) framework.
AI.result: Numerical evaluation on weighted MaxCut instances shows that measurement-guided initialization improves performance of shallow-depth circuits and enables iterative refinement toward high-quality solutions while preserving the non-variational structure of FALQON.
AI.conclusion: Measurement statistics can be effectively exploited to enhance shallow quantum optimization protocols compatible with NISQ devices, demonstrating that measurement-guided approaches can improve performance without requiring classical parameter optimization.

title: A quantum mechanical analysis of the coherence de Broglie wavelength for superresolution and enhanced sensitivity in a coupled interferometer scheme
summary: Quantum sensing has drawn considerable attention as a means to overcome the fundamental limitations in classical sensing. In practice, however, quantum sensing has been strongly constrained by the photon loss, the achievable photon number N in N00N states, and by a finite squeezing level in squeezed states. These limitations are particularly critical to photon-loss-sensitive applications such as LiDAR as well as to general sensing platforms that require large effective N, such as ring-laser gyroscopes. Recently, fundamentally different sensing platforms have been reported to overcome both classical and quantum constraints in a practical regime. One such approach exploits the coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) realized in an anti-symmetrically coupled Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) architecture. Here, a pure quantum mechanical analysis of the CBW is presented for a loss-free sensing mechanism of superresolution with enhanced sensitivity. A proof-of-principle demonstration of CBW is also presented.

AI.tldr: Quantum sensing using coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) in anti-symmetrically coupled Mach-Zehnder interferometer for superresolution sensing with enhanced sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Overcome practical limitations in quantum sensing including photon loss, limited N in N00N states, and finite squeezing levels, particularly critical for photon-loss-sensitive applications like LiDAR and platforms requiring large effective N like ring-laser gyroscopes.
AI.method: Pure quantum mechanical analysis of coherence de Broglie wavelength (CBW) realized in anti-symmetrically coupled Mach-Zehnder interferometer architecture for loss-free sensing mechanism; proof-of-principle demonstration of CBW.
AI.result: Fundamentally different sensing platform that overcomes both classical and quantum constraints in practical regime; achieves superresolution with enhanced sensitivity through CBW approach.
AI.conclusion: CBW approach provides a practical solution to overcome key limitations in quantum sensing, enabling loss-free superresolution sensing with enhanced sensitivity for applications like LiDAR and gyroscopes.

title: A Unified Error Correction Code for Universal Quantum Computing with Identical Particles
comment: The manuscript was submitted to Physical Review Letters on June 13, 2025 (Manuscript ID: LF20042). One of the referee reports stated: In summary, ..., it lacks the broad impact and immediate relevance necessary for Physical Review Letters. I recommend that the manuscript be transferred to a more specialized journal, such as Physical Review A
summary: We present a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture based on identical particle qubits (IPQs), where we find that the first-order IPQ - bath interaction fundamentally differs from the conventional first-order qubit-bath interaction. This key distinction necessitates a redesign of existing strategies to fight decoherence. We propose that the simplest quantum error correction code can be realized directly within the physical qubit, provided that conventional correction and restoration are generalized beyond unitary operations to employ physically implementable reversal operations -- naturally placing logical and physical qubits on equal footing. We further demonstrate that dynamical decoupling (DD) remains effective within this unified framework, and that a decoherence-free subspace (DFS) -- like structure emerges. Unlike previous approximate treatments, our analytically solvable IPQ-Bath model enables rigorous testing of these strategies, with numerical simulations validating their effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture using identical particle qubits with redesigned decoherence-fighting strategies, enabling simplest QEC code within physical qubits and effective dynamical decoupling.
AI.motivation: Identical particle qubits exhibit fundamentally different first-order interactions with baths compared to conventional qubits, requiring redesign of existing decoherence-fighting strategies and enabling new approaches to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.method: Propose universal fault-tolerant architecture using identical particle qubits, generalize quantum error correction beyond unitary operations to physically implementable reversal operations, demonstrate dynamical decoupling effectiveness, and develop analytically solvable IPQ-Bath model for rigorous testing.
AI.result: Simplest quantum error correction code can be realized directly within physical qubits, dynamical decoupling remains effective, decoherence-free subspace-like structure emerges, and numerical simulations validate strategy effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Identical particle qubits enable unified framework where logical and physical qubits are on equal footing, with redesigned decoherence-fighting strategies that are rigorously testable through analytically solvable models.

title: Fundamentals of Quantum Machine Learning and Robustness
comment: This book chapter has been accepted for Springer Nature Quantum Robustness in Artificial Intelligence and will appear in the book: https://link.springer.com/book/9783032111524#accessibility-information
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) sits at the intersection of quantum computing and classical machine learning, offering the prospect of new computational paradigms and advantages for processing complex data. This chapter introduces the fundamentals of QML for readers from both communities, establishing a shared conceptual foundation. We connect the worst-case, adversarial perspective from theoretical computer science with the physical principles of quantum systems, highlighting how superposition, entanglement, and measurement collapse influence learning and robustness. Special attention is given to adversarial robustness, understood as the ability of QML models to resist inputs designed to cause failure. We motivate the study of QML in adversarial settings, outlining distinctions between classical and quantum data and computations when the adversary is a core element. This chapter serves as a starting point to adversarial and robust quantum machine learning in subsequent chapters.

AI.tldr: Introduction to quantum machine learning fundamentals with focus on adversarial robustness, connecting theoretical computer science perspectives with quantum physics principles.
AI.motivation: Establish shared conceptual foundation between quantum computing and classical machine learning communities, highlighting the need to understand adversarial robustness in QML systems where quantum properties like superposition and entanglement affect learning behavior.
AI.method: Connects worst-case adversarial perspective from theoretical computer science with physical principles of quantum systems (superposition, entanglement, measurement collapse), analyzes distinctions between classical and quantum data/computations in adversarial settings.
AI.result: Provides foundational framework for understanding how quantum properties influence learning robustness, establishes conceptual bridge between classical adversarial ML and quantum systems, identifies key distinctions when adversaries are considered in quantum contexts.
AI.conclusion: Serves as introductory chapter establishing fundamentals for subsequent exploration of adversarial and robust quantum machine learning, emphasizing the importance of considering quantum-specific properties in security and robustness analysis.

title: Hilbert Space Black Hole Analog: Unidirectional Transport without Driving
summary: Black holes permit matter to cross their event horizon in only one direction. We show that interacting bosons in optical lattices with asymmetric barrier exhibit an analogous phenomenon, creating unidirectional quantum transport without external driving or dissipation. This directionality emerges purely from many-body interactions, which cause asymmetric projection of the initial state onto transport-enabled or transport-forbidden sectors. The resulting dynamics create an effective one-way boundary in Hilbert space, forming a quantum analog of a black-hole event horizon. Our results establish interactions as a fundamentally new route to directional transport, enabling coherent rectification in atomtronic circuits by the use of intrinsic properties of the system only.

AI.tldr: Interacting bosons in optical lattices with asymmetric barriers create unidirectional quantum transport without external driving, analogous to black hole event horizons, through many-body interactions alone.
AI.motivation: To establish interactions as a fundamentally new route to directional transport, enabling coherent rectification in atomtronic circuits using only intrinsic system properties, without requiring external driving or dissipation.
AI.method: Study interacting bosons in optical lattices with asymmetric barriers, where many-body interactions cause asymmetric projection of initial states onto transport-enabled or transport-forbidden sectors, creating effective one-way boundaries in Hilbert space.
AI.result: The system exhibits unidirectional quantum transport purely from many-body interactions, forming a quantum analog of black-hole event horizons where matter can only cross in one direction.
AI.conclusion: Interactions provide a novel mechanism for directional transport, enabling coherent rectification in atomtronic circuits using intrinsic quantum properties without external control.

title: Aging of coupled qubits
summary: The aging transition refers to the shift from an oscillatory state to a globally ceased state due to some forms of deterioration in classical physics. Similar behavior has also been observed in quantum oscillators. Although it has received extensive attention in coupled oscillator systems, it has not yet been studied in coupled qubits. In this manuscript, we explore the aging transition in a network of coupled qubits. Our model describes {numerous} qubits driven by a laser, with both dissipative and coherent qubit-qubit couplings. The ratio of inactive qubits to total qubits and the population in the excited state of the qubits are employed to characterize the aging transition. We find a transition where the population in the excited states suddenly drops when the ratio exceeds a threshold. This behavior is intriguing and contrasts with coupled oscillators, where no sudden drop is observed. Additionally, we demonstrate how the couplings and driving laser influence the threshold. The underlying physics of the sudden drop is elucidated. The region where the aging transition occurs is determined based on stability analysis theory.

AI.tldr: The paper studies aging transition in coupled qubits, showing a sudden drop in excited state population when inactive qubits exceed a threshold, unlike classical oscillators.
AI.motivation: Aging transition (oscillatory to ceased state) has been studied in classical physics and quantum oscillators but not in coupled qubits. The authors aim to investigate this phenomenon in qubit networks to understand quantum analogs of classical aging transitions.
AI.method: Model of numerous laser-driven qubits with both dissipative and coherent qubit-qubit couplings. Uses ratio of inactive to total qubits and excited state population to characterize aging transition. Employs stability analysis theory to determine transition regions.
AI.result: Discovery of a transition where excited state population suddenly drops when inactive qubit ratio exceeds a threshold. This contrasts with coupled oscillators where no sudden drop occurs. Shows how couplings and driving laser influence the threshold and elucidates underlying physics of the sudden drop.
AI.conclusion: Aging transition occurs in coupled qubits with distinct quantum features, particularly a sudden population drop not seen in classical oscillators. The work establishes quantum analogs of classical aging phenomena and provides theoretical framework for understanding transitions in qubit networks.

title: Distilling Magic States in the Bicycle Architecture
summary:
Magic State Distillation is considered to be one of the promising methods for supplying the non-Clifford resources required to achieve universal fault tolerance. Conventional MSD protocols implemented in surface codes often require multiple code blocks and lattice surgery rounds, resulting in substantial qubit overhead, especially at low target error rates.
  In this work, we present practical magic state distillation factories on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes that execute Pauli-measurement-based Clifford circuits inside a single BB code block. We formulate distillation circuit design as a joint optimization of logical qubit mapping, gate scheduling, measurement nativization, and protocol compression via qubit recycling. Based on detailed resource analysis and simulations, our BB factories have space-time volume comparable to that of leading distillation factories while delivering lower target error at a smaller qubit footprint, and are particularly compelling as second-round distillers following magic state cultivations.

AI.tldr: Practical magic state distillation factories on Bivariate Bicycle codes that execute distillation circuits within a single code block, achieving lower target error with smaller qubit footprint compared to conventional surface code approaches.
AI.motivation: Conventional MSD protocols in surface codes require multiple code blocks and lattice surgery rounds, leading to substantial qubit overhead especially at low target error rates. There's a need for more efficient distillation methods with reduced resource requirements.
AI.method: Implement distillation factories on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes that execute Pauli-measurement-based Clifford circuits inside a single BB code block. Formulate distillation circuit design as joint optimization of logical qubit mapping, gate scheduling, measurement nativization, and protocol compression via qubit recycling.
AI.result: BB factories achieve space-time volume comparable to leading distillation factories while delivering lower target error at smaller qubit footprint. They are particularly effective as second-round distillers following magic state cultivations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BB code-based distillation factories offer a practical and resource-efficient alternative to conventional surface code MSD protocols, especially suitable for low-error magic state distillation with reduced qubit overhead.

title: Assessing the Practical Feasibility of the Clader-Jacobs-Sprouse Quantum Algorithm for Calculating Radar Cross Sections
summary: In 2013, Clader, Jacobs, and Sprouse developed a quantum computing algorithm that solves electromagnetic scattering problems exponentially faster than the best known classical algorithm for that problem. We examine this quantum algorithm's potential practical feasibility for modeling a target's radar cross section. Doing so could be important for modeling and predicting radar behavior against emerging targets.

AI.tldr: Analysis of quantum algorithm's practical feasibility for radar cross section modeling
AI.motivation: To examine the potential practical feasibility of a 2013 quantum algorithm for electromagnetic scattering problems, specifically for modeling radar cross sections of emerging targets to improve radar behavior prediction.
AI.method: Examination and analysis of the quantum algorithm developed by Clader, Jacobs, and Sprouse, focusing on its application to radar cross section modeling problems.
AI.result: The paper examines the algorithm's potential practical feasibility, but the abstract doesn't specify concrete results - it focuses on the importance of such analysis for radar applications.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing the quantum algorithm's practical feasibility for radar cross section modeling could be important for predicting radar behavior against emerging targets, suggesting potential value in further investigation.

title: Effect of atom-oscillator interaction on the aging transition in coupled oscillators
summary: Oscillators are often employed as a model of radiation fields, which may couple to an atom and play an important role for creating and manipulating nonclassical states in quantum metrology, quantum simulation, and quantum information. Aging transitions in coupled oscillators have been studied extensively in both the classical and quantum contexts. It is well known that the onset of aging transitions can be modulated by the dissipative coupling between oscillators. In this study, we propose an alternative way to modulate the aging transition through coherent couplings between a two-level atom and the oscillators. Our findings reveal that, compared to atom-free systems in both classical and quantum regimes, the atom-oscillator coherent interaction reduces the inactive-to-total oscillator ratio required for aging transitions. Analytical results of the transition for both the classical oscillators and quantum oscillators suggest that the decay rate of the atom and the atom-oscillator coupling strength jointly change the aging transition point. The physics behind the observation is also elucidated in this article. Our research introduces a readily implementable strategy for manipulating aging transitions in more intricate systems, thereby advancing the control and understanding of these critical transitions in quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using coherent atom-oscillator coupling to modulate aging transitions, showing it reduces the inactive oscillator ratio needed for transitions compared to atom-free systems.
AI.motivation: Aging transitions in coupled oscillators are important for quantum technologies, but existing modulation methods rely on dissipative coupling. The authors seek an alternative approach using coherent atom-oscillator interactions.
AI.method: The study introduces coherent coupling between a two-level atom and oscillators as an alternative modulation mechanism. Analytical methods are used to analyze aging transitions in both classical and quantum oscillator regimes.
AI.result: Atom-oscillator coherent interaction reduces the inactive-to-total oscillator ratio required for aging transitions compared to atom-free systems. The transition point is jointly determined by atom decay rate and coupling strength.
AI.conclusion: The research provides a readily implementable strategy for manipulating aging transitions in complex systems, advancing control and understanding of these transitions in quantum technologies.

title: Quantum circuit design from a retraction-based Riemannian optimization framework
summary: Designing quantum circuits for ground state preparation is a fundamental task in quantum information science. However, standard Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are often constrained by limited ansatz expressivity and difficult optimization landscapes. To address these issues, we adopt a geometric perspective, formulating the problem as the minimization of an energy cost function directly over the unitary group. We establish a retraction-based Riemannian optimization framework for this setting, ensuring that all algorithmic procedures are implementable on quantum hardware. Within this framework, we unify existing randomized gradient approaches under a Riemannian Random Subspace Gradient Projection (RRSGP) method. While recent geometric approaches have predominantly focused on such first-order gradient descent techniques, efficient second-order methods remain unexplored. To bridge this gap, we derive explicit expressions for the Riemannian Hessian and show that it can be estimated directly on quantum hardware via parameter-shift rules. Building on this, we propose the Riemannian Random Subspace Newton (RRSN) method, a scalable second-order algorithm that constructs a Newton system from measurement data. Numerical simulations indicate that RRSN achieves quadratic convergence, yielding high-precision ground states in significantly fewer iterations compared to both existing first-order approaches and standard VQA baselines. Ultimately, this work provides a systematic foundation for applying a broader class of efficient Riemannian algorithms to quantum circuit design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Riemannian Random Subspace Newton (RRSN), a second-order quantum optimization method that achieves quadratic convergence for ground state preparation, outperforming existing first-order approaches and standard VQAs.
AI.motivation: Standard Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) suffer from limited ansatz expressivity and difficult optimization landscapes. Existing geometric approaches have focused primarily on first-order gradient methods, leaving efficient second-order techniques unexplored for quantum circuit design.
AI.method: The authors adopt a geometric perspective, formulating ground state preparation as minimization over the unitary group. They establish a retraction-based Riemannian optimization framework implementable on quantum hardware. They derive explicit expressions for the Riemannian Hessian and show it can be estimated via parameter-shift rules. They propose the Riemannian Random Subspace Newton (RRSN) method, a scalable second-order algorithm that constructs Newton systems from measurement data.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that RRSN achieves quadratic convergence, yielding high-precision ground states in significantly fewer iterations compared to both existing first-order approaches and standard VQA baselines.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a systematic foundation for applying a broader class of efficient Riemannian algorithms to quantum circuit design, bridging the gap between geometric optimization and quantum hardware implementation.

title: Non-Clifford symmetry protected topological higher-order cluster states in multi-qubit measurement-based quantum computation
summary: A cluster state is a strongly entangled state, which is a source of measurement-based quantum computation. It is generated by applying controlled-Z (CZ) gates to the state $\left\vert ++\cdots +\right\rangle $. It is protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\text{even}}\times \mathbb{Z}_{2}^{ \text{odd}}$ symmetry. By applying general quantum gates to the state $ \left\vert ++\cdots +\right\rangle $, we systematically obtain a general short-range entangled cluster state. If we use a non-Clifford gate such as the controlled phase-shift gate, we obtain a non-Clifford cluster state. Furthermore, if we use the controlled-controlled Z (CCZ) gate instead of the CZ gate, we obtain non-Clifford cluster states with five-body entanglement. We generalize it to the C$^{N}$Z gate, where $(2N+1)$-body entangled states are generated. The $\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\text{even}}\times \mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\text{odd}}$ symmetry is non-Clifford for $N\geq 3$. We demonstrate that there emerge $2^{2N}$ fold degenerate ground states for an open chain, indicating the emergence of $N$ free spins at each edge. They can be used as an $N$-qubit input and an $N$-qubit output in measurement-based quantum computation. We also study the non-invertible symmetry, the Kennedy-Tasaki transformation and the string-order parameter in addition to the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\text{even}}\times \mathbb{Z}_{2}^{\text{odd}}$ symmetry in these models.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically generalizes cluster states for measurement-based quantum computation using various quantum gates beyond CZ gates, generating non-Clifford cluster states with higher-body entanglement and studying their symmetries and edge properties.
AI.motivation: To systematically extend cluster states beyond the standard CZ-generated ones by applying general quantum gates to the |++⋯+⟩ state, enabling the creation of non-Clifford cluster states with higher-body entanglement for enhanced measurement-based quantum computation capabilities.
AI.method: Apply general quantum gates (including non-Clifford gates like controlled phase-shift gates and multi-controlled gates like CCZ and C^NZ) to the initial state |++⋯+⟩ to generate generalized short-range entangled cluster states. Analyze the resulting states' symmetries (including Z_2^even × Z_2^odd symmetry), edge degeneracy, and properties for measurement-based quantum computation.
AI.result: Non-Clifford cluster states with five-body entanglement from CCZ gates and (2N+1)-body entanglement from C^NZ gates. For N≥3, the Z_2^even × Z_2^odd symmetry becomes non-Clifford. Open chains exhibit 2^{2N}-fold degenerate ground states, indicating N free spins at each edge that can serve as N-qubit input/output in measurement-based quantum computation. Additional analysis of non-invertible symmetry, Kennedy-Tasaki transformation, and string-order parameters.
AI.conclusion: The systematic generalization of cluster states using various quantum gates enables the creation of non-Clifford cluster states with higher-body entanglement, providing enhanced resources for measurement-based quantum computation with multiple qubits at each edge and novel symmetry properties.

title: First- and Second-Order Digital Quantum Simulation of Three-Level Jaynes-Cummings Dynamics on Superconducting Quantum Processors
summary: This work presents a digital quantum simulation of a three-level atomic system interacting with a single-mode electromagnetic field based on the Jaynes-Cummings model, implemented on IBM Quantum superconducting processors. A qutrit is encoded using two physical qubits to represent the atomic states, while an additional qubit encodes the truncated field mode, enabling the realization of effective $Λ$-type atomic dynamics.The continuous-time light-matter interaction is implemented in a digital form by discretizing the evolution using Suzuki-Trotter decomposition. In contrast to an analog realization, the digital simulation replaces the continuous evolution with a sequence of quantum gates whose parameters are explicitly controlled. Phase evolution arising from the interaction Hamiltonian is digitally encoded using calibrated $R_Z$ gates, whose rotation angles are fixed by the physically relevant coupling scale and the chosen Trotter time step.State preparation is achieved using Hadamard and parametrized rotation gates, while the interaction dynamics are implemented through controlled operations. A comparative analysis between first- and second-order Trotter implementations reveals a trade-off between digital accuracy and hardware-induced noise. Overall, the results demonstrate that calibrated gate operations and noise-aware circuit design enable reliable digital simulation of multi-level light-matter interactions on noisy intermediate-scale quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: Digital quantum simulation of three-level atom-field interaction using Jaynes-Cummings model on IBM quantum processors, with qutrit encoded in two qubits and field in one qubit, implemented via Suzuki-Trotter decomposition and calibrated gates.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate reliable digital quantum simulation of multi-level light-matter interactions on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) platforms, specifically implementing Λ-type atomic dynamics from the Jaynes-Cummings model.
AI.method: Encoded qutrit using two physical qubits for atomic states and one qubit for truncated field mode; implemented continuous-time interaction digitally via Suzuki-Trotter decomposition with calibrated R_Z gates; used state preparation with Hadamard and parametrized rotation gates; implemented dynamics through controlled operations; compared first- and second-order Trotter implementations.
AI.result: Comparative analysis revealed trade-off between digital accuracy and hardware-induced noise; demonstrated that calibrated gate operations and noise-aware circuit design enable reliable digital simulation of multi-level light-matter interactions on NISQ platforms.
AI.conclusion: Digital quantum simulation using calibrated gates and noise-aware design is feasible for simulating complex light-matter interactions on current quantum hardware, with careful consideration of Trotter order balancing accuracy against noise accumulation.

title: Qudit stabiliser codes for $\mathbb{Z}_N$ lattice gauge theories with matter
summary: In this work we extend the connection between Quantum Error Correction (QEC) and Lattice Gauge Theories (LGTs) by showing that a $\mathbb{Z}_N$ gauge theory with prime dimension $N$ coupled to dynamical matter can be expressed as a qudit stabilizer code. Using the stabilizer formalism we show how to formulate an exact mapping of the encoded $\mathbb{Z}_N$ gauge theory onto two different bosonic models, uncovering a logical duality generated by error correction itself. From this perspective, quantum error correction provides a unifying language to expose dual descriptions of lattice gauge theories. In addition, we generalize earlier $\mathbb{Z}_2$ constructions on qubits to $\mathbb{Z}_N$ on $N$-level qudits and demonstrate how universal fault-tolerant gates can be implemented via state injection between compatible qudit codes.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a connection between ℤₙ gauge theories with prime N and qudit stabilizer codes, showing that error correction generates logical dualities and enables fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.motivation: To extend the connection between Quantum Error Correction (QEC) and Lattice Gauge Theories (LGTs) beyond the ℤ₂ case, exploring how QEC provides a unifying framework for understanding dual descriptions of gauge theories and enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.method: Using stabilizer formalism to express ℤₙ gauge theory with prime N coupled to dynamical matter as a qudit stabilizer code, formulating exact mappings to bosonic models, and demonstrating how error correction generates logical dualities. Generalizing ℤ₂ constructions to ℤₙ on N-level qudits and implementing universal fault-tolerant gates via state injection between compatible qudit codes.
AI.result: Established that ℤₙ gauge theories with prime N can be expressed as qudit stabilizer codes, uncovered a logical duality generated by error correction itself, and demonstrated implementation of universal fault-tolerant gates via state injection between compatible qudit codes.
AI.conclusion: Quantum error correction provides a unifying language to expose dual descriptions of lattice gauge theories, connecting gauge theory dualities with error correction procedures, and enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation through qudit code constructions.

title: Task Concurrency and Compatibility in Measurement-Based Quantum Networks
comment: To be published in 2026 International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
summary: Measurement-Based Quantum Networks (MBQNs) rely on multipartite pre-shared entanglement resources to satisfy entanglement requests. Traditional designs optimize these resources for individual tasks, neglecting that multiple tasks may arrive concurrently and compete for the same entanglement. We introduce compatibility as a design-level metric, capturing whether concurrent tasks can be satisfied by the same entanglement resources. We define a worst-case notion of compatibility where nodes are prevented from coordinating after task arrival and illustrate why tasks may be incompatible. Furthermore, we explore compatibility extensions that account for stochastic arrivals and the capability to supplement the pre-shared entanglement with additional entanglement on-demand, and show that incompatibility differs structurally dependent on the set of concurrent tasks. We argue that compatibility should be used for resource state design, building the foundation for determining which task pairs the network should support with pre-shared entanglement and which require execution-time coordination. Numerical simulations demonstrate this potential, with $(G,1)$-compatibility achieving a 40%-55% gain in simultaneously supported tasks relative to the single-task baseline. By incorporating compatibility as a fundamental design objective, quantum networks can move beyond single-task optimization towards scalable, robust architectures that effectively balance proactive entanglement distribution and supplemental reactive coordination.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "compatibility" as a design metric for Measurement-Based Quantum Networks to optimize entanglement resources for concurrent tasks, showing 40-55% gains over single-task baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional MBQN designs optimize entanglement resources for individual tasks, ignoring that multiple concurrent tasks may compete for the same resources, leading to inefficiencies and scalability limitations.
AI.method: Introduces compatibility as a design-level metric to determine if concurrent tasks can be satisfied by the same entanglement resources. Defines worst-case compatibility where nodes cannot coordinate after task arrival, explores stochastic arrivals and on-demand entanglement supplementation extensions.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show (G,1)-compatibility achieves 40%-55% gain in simultaneously supported tasks relative to single-task baseline. Demonstrates structural differences in incompatibility based on concurrent task sets.
AI.conclusion: Compatibility should be used as a fundamental design objective for quantum networks to move beyond single-task optimization toward scalable, robust architectures that balance proactive entanglement distribution with reactive coordination.

title: Spatial Entanglement Sudden Death in Spin Chains at All Temperatures
summary: We prove a finite entanglement length for the Gibbs state of any local Hamiltonian on a spin chain at any finite temperature: After removing an interval of size at least equal to the entanglement length, the remaining left and right half-chains are in a separable state.

AI.tldr: Finite entanglement length proven for Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians on spin chains at finite temperature, with separable states after removing interval of entanglement length size.
AI.motivation: To establish rigorous bounds on entanglement in thermal states of quantum spin chains, specifically proving that entanglement has finite range at any finite temperature for local Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Mathematical proof establishing that for any local Hamiltonian on a spin chain, the Gibbs state at finite temperature has finite entanglement length, meaning that after removing an interval of at least this length, the remaining left and right half-chains become separable.
AI.result: Proven existence of finite entanglement length for Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians on spin chains at any finite temperature, with explicit bound that entanglement decays exponentially with distance beyond this length.
AI.conclusion: Thermal states in one-dimensional quantum systems have finite-range entanglement, providing fundamental insight into the structure of quantum correlations at finite temperature and enabling more efficient classical simulations of thermal states.

title: A note on entanglement detection via the generalized realignment moments
summary: The experimental detection of quantum entanglement is of great importance in quantum information processing. We present two separability criteria based on the generalized realignment moments. By incorporating additional parameters, these criteria prove to be more flexible and stronger than some of existing ones. Detailed examples are given to demonstrate their availability and feasibility for entanglement detection.

AI.tldr: Two new separability criteria for quantum entanglement detection based on generalized realignment moments with additional parameters, offering improved flexibility and strength over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Experimental detection of quantum entanglement is crucial for quantum information processing, necessitating improved separability criteria that are more flexible and stronger than existing methods.
AI.method: Developed two separability criteria based on generalized realignment moments, incorporating additional parameters to enhance flexibility and detection capability.
AI.result: The proposed criteria are more flexible and stronger than some existing entanglement detection methods, with detailed examples demonstrating their availability and feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The generalized realignment moments approach provides effective new tools for quantum entanglement detection with improved performance characteristics.

title: Generative Deep Learning for the Two-Dimensional Quantum Rotor Model
summary: The advancement of diverse generative deep learning models and their variants has furnished substantial insights for investigating quantum many-body problems. In this work, we design two models based on the foundational architecture of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to investigate the ground-state properties and phase transition characteristics of the two-dimensional quantum rotor model (QRM). Within a semi-supervised learning framework, we incorporate multiple layers of transposed convolutions in the generator, enabling the conditional GAN to more efficiently extract low-dimensional encoded information. Analysis of one-dimensional latent variables associated with ground-state samples for different system sizes allows us to pinpoint the location of the critical point. In addition, we introduce dynamically adaptive weighting factors related to the distributional characteristics into the loss function of the deep convolutional GAN, and utilize upsampling techniques to enlarge the generated sample sizes. Comparisons of the optimization processes for mean magnetization and potential energy density across different magnetization regimes of QRM demonstrate that our model can efficiently generate valid ground-state samples, significantly reducing computational time. Our results highlight the promising potential of generative deep learning in quantum phase transition research, especially in critical point identification and the auxiliary generation of simulation data for quantum many-body models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two GAN-based models to study ground-state properties and phase transitions in the 2D quantum rotor model, using semi-supervised learning with transposed convolutions and adaptive loss functions to efficiently generate valid ground-state samples and identify critical points.
AI.motivation: To leverage generative deep learning models (particularly GAN variants) for investigating quantum many-body problems, specifically the ground-state properties and phase transition characteristics of the 2D quantum rotor model, aiming to reduce computational time while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Two GAN-based models: 1) A conditional GAN with multiple transposed convolution layers in the generator within a semi-supervised learning framework to extract low-dimensional encoded information; 2) A deep convolutional GAN with dynamically adaptive weighting factors in the loss function and upsampling techniques to enlarge generated sample sizes. Analysis of one-dimensional latent variables for different system sizes to identify critical points.
AI.result: The models efficiently generate valid ground-state samples, significantly reducing computational time. Analysis of latent variables allows precise identification of critical points in the quantum rotor model. Comparisons of optimization processes for mean magnetization and potential energy density across different magnetization regimes demonstrate model effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Generative deep learning shows promising potential for quantum phase transition research, particularly in critical point identification and auxiliary generation of simulation data for quantum many-body models, offering computational efficiency advantages over traditional methods.

title: Toward speedup without quantum coherent access
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2504.00833
summary: Along with the development of quantum technology, finding useful applications of quantum computers has been a central pursuit. Despite various quantum algorithms have been developed, many of them often require strong input assumptions, which is hardware demanding. In particular, recent advances on dequantization have revealed that the quantum advantage is more of a mere artifact of strong input assumptions. In this work, we propose a variant of these algorithms, leveraging both classical and quantum resources. Provided the classical knowledge (the entries) of the matrix/vector of interest, a classical procedure is used to pre-process this information. Then they are fed into a quantum circuit which is shown to be a block encoding of the matrix of interest. From this block-encoding, we show how to use it to tackle a wide range of problems, including principal component analysis, linear equation solving, Hamiltonian simulation, preparing ground state, and data fitting. We also analyze our protocol, showing that both the classical and quantum procedure can achieve logarithmic complexity in the input dimension, thus implying its potential for near term realization. We then discuss several implications and corollaries of our result. First,, our results suggest there are certain matrices/Hamiltonians where our method can provide exponential improvement compared to the existing ones with respect to the sparsity. Regarding dense linear systems, our method achieves exponential speed-up with respect to the inverse of error tolerance, compared to the best previously known quantum algorithm for dense systems. Last, and most importantly, regarding quantum data fitting, we show how the output of our quantum algorithms can be leveraged to predict unseen data. Thus, it provides an end-to-end application, which has been an open aspect of the previous quantum data fitting algorithm.

AI.tldr: A hybrid classical-quantum algorithm framework that uses classical pre-processing of matrix/vector entries to create efficient block encodings, enabling logarithmic complexity for various problems including PCA, linear systems, Hamiltonian simulation, and data fitting with exponential improvements in certain cases.
AI.motivation: To address the hardware demands and strong input assumptions of existing quantum algorithms, and to overcome limitations revealed by dequantization results showing quantum advantage may be an artifact of these assumptions. The goal is to develop practical quantum-classical hybrid methods suitable for near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: A hybrid approach where classical knowledge of matrix/vector entries is pre-processed classically, then fed into a quantum circuit that creates a block encoding of the matrix. This block encoding is then used to solve various problems including principal component analysis, linear equation solving, Hamiltonian simulation, ground state preparation, and data fitting.
AI.result: Achieves logarithmic complexity in input dimension for both classical and quantum procedures, enabling near-term realization. Provides exponential improvement for certain matrices/Hamiltonians compared to existing methods with respect to sparsity, exponential speed-up for dense linear systems with respect to error tolerance, and enables end-to-end quantum data fitting with prediction capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid classical-quantum framework offers practical advantages for near-term quantum computing by leveraging classical pre-processing to reduce quantum resource requirements, achieving significant speed-ups for various problems while providing an end-to-end solution for quantum data fitting applications.

title: Quantum coherence of mixed states under noisy channels in noninertial frames
summary: We focus our attention on tripartite mixed states as initial states, and apply coherence concurrence to investigate quantum coherence properties in the background of a Schwarzschild black hole under phase damping, phase flip and bit flip channels, respectively. Several analytic complementary relationships based on coherence concurrence for tripartite subsystems are proposed. In the case of the bit flip channel, the behavior of the coherence concurrence is similar to the one of the phase damping channel, the accessible coherence concurrence always degrades as the Hawking acceleration rising, but sudden death never occurs, while the inaccessible coherence increases from zero monotonically. Interestingly, the coherence concurrence is decreasing at first and then increasing as the decay probability rising under phase flip channel. Unlike the case of tripartite pure states, the coherence concurrence of mixed state with X shape is equal to $l_1$ -norm of coherence.

AI.tldr: Analysis of quantum coherence properties for tripartite mixed states in Schwarzschild black hole background under various quantum channels, revealing different coherence concurrence behaviors.
AI.motivation: To investigate how quantum coherence properties of tripartite mixed states evolve in the curved spacetime of a Schwarzschild black hole under different quantum noise channels (phase damping, phase flip, and bit flip), and to establish complementary relationships for coherence concurrence in tripartite subsystems.
AI.method: Apply coherence concurrence measure to analyze tripartite mixed states in Schwarzschild black hole background under three quantum channels: phase damping, phase flip, and bit flip. Derive analytic complementary relationships for coherence concurrence in tripartite subsystems and compare behaviors across different channels.
AI.result: 1) For bit flip channel: coherence concurrence degrades with increasing Hawking acceleration but never experiences sudden death; inaccessible coherence increases monotonically from zero. 2) For phase flip channel: coherence concurrence shows non-monotonic behavior - decreasing first then increasing with rising decay probability. 3) Unlike tripartite pure states, coherence concurrence of X-shaped mixed states equals l₁-norm of coherence.
AI.conclusion: Quantum coherence properties of tripartite mixed states exhibit channel-dependent behaviors in Schwarzschild black hole background. The study reveals important complementary relationships and shows that coherence concurrence can behave differently under various quantum channels, with some channels preserving coherence better than others despite Hawking radiation effects.

title: Quantum discord of mixed states under noisy channels in the curved spacetime
summary: We focus our attention on two-qubit mixed states as initial states, and apply the geometric measure of quantum discord to investigate quantum discord properties in the background of a Schwarzschild black hole under phase damping, phase flip and bit flip channels, respectively. Several analytical complementary relationships based on quantum discords for bipartite subsystems are proposed. For the three channel noises, the behaviors of discords are similar, the accessible discords always degrade as the Hawking acceleration rising, but sudden death never occurs, while the inaccessible discords increase from zero monotonically. Interestingly, in the case of the bit flip channel and phase flip channel, the discords perform symmetrically with the decay probability rising.
