AI.tldr: Analysis of quantum discord dynamics for two-qubit mixed states in Schwarzschild black hole background under phase damping, phase flip, and bit flip channels, revealing degradation of accessible discord with Hawking acceleration but no sudden death.
AI.motivation: To investigate how quantum discord properties evolve for bipartite quantum systems in curved spacetime (Schwarzschild black hole background) when subjected to different types of quantum noise channels (phase damping, phase flip, bit flip).
AI.method: Apply geometric measure of quantum discord to two-qubit mixed states in Schwarzschild black hole background, analyze under three channel noises: phase damping, phase flip, and bit flip channels. Propose analytical complementary relationships for bipartite subsystems based on quantum discords.
AI.result: For all three channel noises: accessible discords degrade as Hawking acceleration increases (no sudden death occurs); inaccessible discords increase monotonically from zero. For bit flip and phase flip channels, discords show symmetric behavior with rising decay probability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum discord exhibits consistent degradation patterns under Hawking acceleration across different noise channels, with accessible discord decreasing and inaccessible discord increasing, revealing fundamental relationships between quantum correlations and curved spacetime effects.

title: Mach-Zehnder interferometer for in-situ characterization of atom traps
summary: Manipulating cold atoms in traps is a key tool for numerous realizations of quantum simulators and quantum sensors. They require accurate modeling and characterization of the underlying trapping potentials. We introduce a technique based on the Mach-Zehnder interferometer for in-situ characterization of weakly anharmonic potentials. By simulating the interferometer in an optical dipole trap, we can accurately determine its trap frequency and upper bounds onto anharmonicity magnitudes.

AI.tldr: Technique using Mach-Zehnder interferometer for in-situ characterization of weakly anharmonic optical dipole trap potentials, enabling accurate trap frequency determination and anharmonicity bounds.
AI.motivation: Cold atom manipulation in traps is essential for quantum simulators and sensors, requiring accurate modeling and characterization of trapping potentials, particularly for weakly anharmonic potentials.
AI.method: Introduces a technique based on Mach-Zehnder interferometer for in-situ characterization. Simulates the interferometer in an optical dipole trap to analyze potential properties.
AI.result: Enables accurate determination of trap frequency and establishes upper bounds on anharmonicity magnitudes for weakly anharmonic potentials.
AI.conclusion: The Mach-Zehnder interferometer-based technique provides effective in-situ characterization of weakly anharmonic trapping potentials, supporting improved modeling for quantum simulation and sensing applications.

title: Simulating Microwave-Controlled Spin Imaging with Free-Space Electrons
summary: Coherent spin resonance techniques, such as nuclear and electron spin resonance spectroscopy, have revolutionized non-invasive imaging by providing spectrally resolved information about spin dynamics. Motivated by the recent emergence of electron microscopy methods capable of sensing microwave-excitations, we establish a theoretical framework for Spin Resonance Spectroscopy (SRS) in transmission electron microscopy (TEM). This technique combines microwave pump fields with focused electron probe beams to enable state-selective spin imaging at the atomic scale. Using scattering theory, we model the interaction between free-space electrons and electron spin systems, capturing both elastic and inelastic processes. The strongest effect of the spin system on the free electron is a magnetic phase shift. Our simulations demonstrate that phase shifts from individual electron spins are detectable in both image mode and diffraction mode. In principle, differential measurements under microwave control allow the extraction of local resonance frequencies that are influenced by the surrounding spin environment. By evaluating the Classical Fisher Information (CFI), we identify imaging conditions that maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), showing how defocus and beam width affect the measurement sensitivity. These findings establish a foundation for integrating SRS with high-resolution TEM, bridging spin spectroscopy and atomic-scale imaging, and enabling new capabilities in quantum spin research and nanoscale materials characterization.

AI.tldr: Theoretical framework for Spin Resonance Spectroscopy in TEM combining microwave fields with electron beams for atomic-scale spin imaging, showing detectable phase shifts from individual electron spins.
AI.motivation: Recent emergence of electron microscopy methods capable of sensing microwave excitations motivates development of theoretical framework for integrating spin resonance spectroscopy with transmission electron microscopy to enable atomic-scale spin imaging.
AI.method: Established theoretical framework using scattering theory to model interaction between free-space electrons and electron spin systems, capturing both elastic and inelastic processes. Used Classical Fisher Information to identify optimal imaging conditions maximizing signal-to-noise ratio.
AI.result: Simulations demonstrate detectable phase shifts from individual electron spins in both image and diffraction modes. Differential measurements under microwave control can extract local resonance frequencies influenced by surrounding spin environment. Defocus and beam width significantly affect measurement sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Establishes foundation for integrating Spin Resonance Spectroscopy with high-resolution TEM, bridging spin spectroscopy and atomic-scale imaging, enabling new capabilities in quantum spin research and nanoscale materials characterization.

title: $σ$-VQE: Excited-state preparation of quantum many-body scars with shallow circuits
summary: We present and benchmark a type of variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), which we denote the $σ$-VQE. It is designed to target mid-spectrum eigenstates and prepare quantum many-body scar states. The approach leverages the fact that noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices are limited in their ability to generate generic highly-entangled states. This modified VQE pairs a low-depth circuit with an energy-selective objective that explicitly penalizes energy variance around a chosen target energy. The cost function exploits the limited expressibility of the shallow circuit as atypical low-entanglement eigenstates such as scar states are preferentially selected. We validate this mechanism across two complementary families of models that contain many-body scar states: the Shiraishi-Mori embedding approach, and the matrix-product state parent Hamiltonian construction. We define an unbiased estimation scheme for the nonlinear cost function that is compatible with qubit-wise commuting grouping and bitstring reuse. A proof-of-principle demonstration using a small-system instance was carried out on IBM Fez (Heron r2 QPU). These results motivate its use both as a practical "scar detector" and as a state-preparation primitive for initializing nonthermal eigenstate-supported dynamics.

AI.tldr: σ-VQE is a modified variational quantum eigensolver that targets mid-spectrum eigenstates and prepares quantum many-body scar states using shallow circuits and an energy-selective objective that penalizes energy variance.
AI.motivation: To leverage the limitations of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices in generating generic highly-entangled states, and to develop a practical method for targeting atypical low-entanglement eigenstates like many-body scar states that are more accessible to shallow circuits.
AI.method: Modified VQE approach using low-depth circuits paired with an energy-selective objective function that explicitly penalizes energy variance around a chosen target energy. The method exploits limited circuit expressibility to preferentially select low-entanglement eigenstates. Includes unbiased estimation scheme for nonlinear cost function compatible with qubit-wise commuting grouping and bitstring reuse.
AI.result: Validated across two families of models containing many-body scar states: Shiraishi-Mori embedding approach and matrix-product state parent Hamiltonian construction. Demonstrated proof-of-principle on IBM Fez (Heron r2 QPU) for small-system instances.
AI.conclusion: σ-VQE serves as both a practical "scar detector" and a state-preparation primitive for initializing nonthermal eigenstate-supported dynamics, making it suitable for NISQ devices.

title: Error correction with brickwork Clifford circuits
comment: 24 pages, see also the related work of Liu et al. (specifically the journal version [PRX Quantum 7, 010331 (2026)])
summary: We prove that random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits form (in expectation) good approximate quantum error correction codes in logarithmic depth. Our proof makes use of the statistical mechanics techniques for random circuits developed by Dalzell et al. [PRX Quantum 3, 010333], adapted extensively to our own purpose. We also consider exact error correction, where we give matching upper and lower bounds for the required depth in which random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits become error correcting.

AI.tldr: Random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits form good approximate quantum error correction codes in logarithmic depth, with matching upper and lower bounds for exact error correction.
AI.motivation: To understand the error correction capabilities of random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits and determine the minimal depth required for them to function as quantum error correction codes.
AI.method: Uses statistical mechanics techniques for random circuits developed by Dalzell et al., adapted to analyze random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits. Considers both approximate and exact error correction scenarios.
AI.result: Random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits form good approximate quantum error correction codes in logarithmic depth (in expectation). For exact error correction, matching upper and lower bounds are provided for the required depth.
AI.conclusion: Random 1D Clifford brickwork circuits can serve as effective quantum error correction codes with surprisingly shallow depth, demonstrating the power of random circuit architectures for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Enhancing low-temperature quantum thermometry and magnetometry via quadratic interactions in optomechanical-like systems
summary: Standard optomechanical sensors operating in the low-temperature regime often face fundamental precision limits imposed by vacuum fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate that moving beyond conventional radiation-pressure interactions and exploiting quadratic coupling can surpass these limits, generating intrinsic squeezing and non-Gaussian features in the probe state. We study quantum thermometry and magnetometry in a coupled two-resonator system, focusing on the estimation of a thermal bath temperature and an external magnetic field. The resonators are assumed to be in thermal equilibrium with a common bath, while a weak magnetic field acts on one of the resonators. We perform measurements on a single resonator, which serves as the probe for estimating both parameters. We compute the quantum Fisher information of the probe for two different interaction models between the resonators. Our results show that the counter-rotating terms in the quadratic interaction naturally induce squeezing at intermediate coupling and strong non-Gaussian correlations as the coupling increases further. These effects yield orders-of-magnitude enhancement in sensitivity in the low-temperature and weak-field regimes compared to standard radiation-pressure couplings. Finally, we investigate multiparameter estimation and find that, although the optimal measurements remain compatible, statistical correlations between parameters prevent the simultaneous estimation of temperature and magnetic field from attaining single-parameter precision.

AI.tldr: Quadratic optomechanical coupling enables quantum-enhanced sensing beyond vacuum fluctuation limits via intrinsic squeezing and non-Gaussian correlations, significantly improving thermometry and magnetometry sensitivity in low-temperature/weak-field regimes.
AI.motivation: Standard optomechanical sensors face fundamental precision limits from vacuum fluctuations in low-temperature regimes. The paper aims to surpass these limits by moving beyond conventional radiation-pressure interactions to exploit quadratic coupling.
AI.method: Study quantum thermometry and magnetometry in a coupled two-resonator system. One resonator serves as probe for estimating thermal bath temperature and external magnetic field. Compute quantum Fisher information for two different interaction models between resonators, analyzing effects of counter-rotating terms in quadratic interaction.
AI.result: Quadratic interaction induces squeezing at intermediate coupling and strong non-Gaussian correlations at stronger coupling, yielding orders-of-magnitude sensitivity enhancement in low-temperature/weak-field regimes compared to standard radiation-pressure couplings. Multiparameter estimation shows statistical correlations prevent simultaneous estimation from attaining single-parameter precision despite compatible optimal measurements.
AI.conclusion: Quadratic optomechanical coupling provides a pathway to surpass fundamental quantum limits in sensing through generation of squeezing and non-Gaussian features, enabling significant sensitivity improvements for quantum thermometry and magnetometry applications.

title: Experimental Asynchronous Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Cryptographic Conferencing
summary: The quantum cryptographic conferencing (QCC) protocol, which distributes identical secure keys to user groups, is a crucial component of the quantum network. Previous experimental works have implemented the measurement-device-independent (MDI) QCC, of which the key rate in an $N$-user network scales down as $R\sim O(η^N)$, respectively. Building on the MDI QCC protocol, the asynchronous MDI (AMDI) QCC protocol theoretically integrates the mode pairing scheme into QCC, significantly boosting the key rate to $R\sim O(η)$, which is independent of the number of users, and thus demonstrating greater application potential. Experimentally, in this work, we implement the three-user AMDI QCC network without global phase tracking by adopting the fast Fourier transform-based frequency difference estimation and the phase drift compensation technique. Finally, we achieve a key rate of about $4.470\times10^{-9}$ bits per pulse under a maximum overall loss of about 59.6 dB. This work provides a scalable solution for the development of large-scale quantum communication networks in the future.

AI.tldr: Experimental implementation of asynchronous measurement-device-independent quantum cryptographic conferencing (AMDI QCC) with 3 users achieves key rate independent of user count, overcoming previous exponential scaling limitations.
AI.motivation: Previous MDI QCC protocols suffer from key rates that scale exponentially with the number of users (R∼O(η^N)), limiting practical scalability for large quantum networks. The AMDI QCC protocol theoretically offers key rates independent of user count (R∼O(η)), but requires experimental validation.
AI.method: Implemented 3-user AMDI QCC network without global phase tracking using: 1) Fast Fourier transform-based frequency difference estimation, and 2) Phase drift compensation technique. The protocol integrates mode pairing scheme into QCC framework.
AI.result: Achieved key rate of approximately 4.470×10^-9 bits per pulse under maximum overall loss of about 59.6 dB. Demonstrated practical implementation of AMDI QCC with key rate independent of user count.
AI.conclusion: The experimental realization of AMDI QCC provides a scalable solution for future large-scale quantum communication networks by overcoming the exponential key rate scaling limitation of previous protocols.

title: Adversarial Information Gain in Non-ideal Quantum Measurements
summary: Performing a quantum measurement yields two different results: a classical outcome drawn from a probability distribution, according to Born's rule, and a quantum outcome corresponding to the post-measurement state. Quantum devices that provide both outcomes can be described through quantum instruments. In a realistic scenario, one can expect that the observer's obtained classical and quantum outcomes are non-ideal: this can be due to experimental limitations, but could also be explained by adversarial interference, that is, a second party that disturbs the device through a concealed measurement to obtain information. The second scenario can be interpreted through quantum compatibility, as it implies that both the observer's instrument and the adversary's measurement can be performed simultaneously. In this work, we show how the noise of the observer's device relates to the amount of information that the adversary can obtain. We study scenarios in which the adversary aims to acquire information on the same basis as the observer's measurement, or on a mutually unbiased basis with respect to the observer's basis. In both cases, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the compatibility of a single qubit non-ideal quantum instrument and a noisy meter, from which we obtain the maximum amount of information that the adversary can extract in terms of the noise parameters of the observer's instrument. Finally, we provide the device implementation from the adversary's point of view for the same basis scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how noise in quantum measurement devices relates to information leakage to adversaries, deriving compatibility conditions between observer's instruments and adversary's measurements for single-qubit systems.
AI.motivation: Realistic quantum measurements produce non-ideal outcomes due to experimental limitations or adversarial interference. The paper aims to quantify how device noise affects the amount of information an adversary can extract, particularly when the adversary tries to measure in the same basis or a mutually unbiased basis relative to the observer.
AI.method: The authors use quantum instrument formalism to describe measurement devices providing both classical outcomes and post-measurement states. They study compatibility conditions between the observer's non-ideal quantum instrument and an adversary's noisy meter. They derive necessary and sufficient conditions for single-qubit systems and analyze scenarios where the adversary measures in the same basis or a mutually unbiased basis.
AI.result: The paper derives explicit compatibility conditions for single-qubit non-ideal quantum instruments and noisy meters. It quantifies the maximum information an adversary can extract in terms of the observer's instrument noise parameters. For the same-basis scenario, the authors provide the device implementation from the adversary's perspective.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a direct relationship between quantum measurement device noise and information leakage to adversaries. It provides analytical tools to assess security vulnerabilities in quantum measurement scenarios and offers implementation guidance for adversarial measurement strategies in same-basis attacks.

title: Quantum-limited detection of arrival time and carrier frequency of time-dependent signals
summary: Precise measurements of both the arrival time and carrier frequency of light pulses are essential for time-frequency-encoded quantum technologies. Quantum mechanics, however, imposes fundamental limits on the simultaneous determination of these quantities. In this work, we derive and experimentally verify the quantum uncertainty bounds governing joint time-frequency measurements. We show that when detection is restricted to finite time windows, the problem is naturally described by a quantum rotor, rendering the commonly used Heisenberg uncertainty relation inapplicable. We further propose an optimal detection scheme that saturates these fundamental limits. By sampling the Q-function, we demonstrate the reconstruction of the Wigner function beyond the harmonic oscillator. Using an experimental implementation based on a quantum pulse gate, we confirm that the proposed scheme approaches the ultimate quantum limit for simultaneous time-frequency measurements. These results provide a new framework for joint time-frequency detection with direct implications for precision measurements and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Quantum uncertainty bounds for joint time-frequency measurements are derived and experimentally verified, showing that finite time windows require a quantum rotor description rather than the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, with an optimal scheme approaching the ultimate quantum limit.
AI.motivation: Precise simultaneous measurement of arrival time and carrier frequency of light pulses is essential for time-frequency-encoded quantum technologies, but quantum mechanics imposes fundamental limits on joint determination of these quantities.
AI.method: Derived quantum uncertainty bounds for joint time-frequency measurements, showing finite time windows require quantum rotor description; proposed optimal detection scheme that saturates fundamental limits; used Q-function sampling to reconstruct Wigner function beyond harmonic oscillator; implemented experimental setup based on quantum pulse gate.
AI.result: Experimental verification confirms proposed scheme approaches ultimate quantum limit for simultaneous time-frequency measurements; quantum rotor description is necessary for finite time windows; optimal scheme saturates fundamental bounds.
AI.conclusion: Provides new framework for joint time-frequency detection with direct implications for precision measurements and quantum information processing, establishing fundamental quantum limits and optimal measurement strategies.

title: Entanglement-Induced Resilience of Quantum Dynamics
summary: Quantum many-body devices suffer from imperfections that destabilize dynamics and limit scalability. We show that the dynamical growth of entanglement can intrinsically protect generic quantum dynamics against coherent and perturbative noise. Through rigorous theoretical analysis of general quantum dynamics and numerical simulations of spin chains and fermionic lattices, we prove that entanglement-entropy growth confines the influence of local Hamiltonian perturbations, thereby suppressing errors in dynamical errors. The degree of protection correlates quantitatively with the entanglement entropy of subsystems on which the perturbations act, and applies broadly to both analog quantum simulators and real-time control protocols. This entanglement-induced resilience is conceptually distinct from quantum error correction or dynamical decoupling: it passively leverages native many-body correlations without additional qubits, measurements, or control overhead. Our results reveal a generic mechanism linking entanglement growth to dynamical stability and provide practical guidelines for designing noise-resilient quantum devices.

AI.tldr: Entanglement growth intrinsically protects quantum dynamics against noise by confining the influence of local perturbations, without requiring additional resources like error correction or dynamical decoupling.
AI.motivation: Quantum many-body devices suffer from imperfections that destabilize dynamics and limit scalability, creating a need for intrinsic protection mechanisms that don't require additional resources.
AI.method: Rigorous theoretical analysis of general quantum dynamics combined with numerical simulations of spin chains and fermionic lattices to study how entanglement-entropy growth confines local Hamiltonian perturbations.
AI.result: Entanglement growth quantitatively suppresses errors by confining the influence of local perturbations, with protection degree correlating with entanglement entropy of affected subsystems; applies to both analog simulators and real-time control protocols.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement-induced resilience provides a generic mechanism linking entanglement growth to dynamical stability, offering practical guidelines for designing noise-resilient quantum devices without additional qubits, measurements, or control overhead.

title: Characterization-free classification and identification of the environment between two quantum players
summary: Classifying the causal structure of quantum channels is essential for verifying quantum networks and certifying quantum resources. We introduce a characterization-free protocol enabling two isolated players, Alice and Bob, to classify and identify the definite-order strategy adopted by an unknown environment mediating their channels. Without assuming knowledge of their devices or the environment, the players infer the causal order solely from input-output statistics by testing Markovian conditions that we prove are necessary and sufficient for each strategy class. Remarkably, we prove that even with a minimal random channel consisting of two-outcome POVMs and two-state preparations, the protocol retains full performance with probability one. We experimentally demonstrate the protocol on an optical platform, reliably distinguishing between several strategies. Our results provide a strong and robust tool for causal inference in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: Protocol for classifying causal structure of quantum channels without device knowledge using input-output statistics and Markovian conditions, proven effective even with minimal random channels and experimentally demonstrated.
AI.motivation: Classifying causal structure of quantum channels is essential for verifying quantum networks and certifying quantum resources, but current methods often require device knowledge or specific characterizations.
AI.method: Characterization-free protocol where two isolated players (Alice and Bob) classify definite-order strategies of unknown environment using input-output statistics by testing Markovian conditions that are proven necessary and sufficient for each strategy class.
AI.result: Protocol retains full performance with probability one even with minimal random channels (two-outcome POVMs and two-state preparations). Experimental demonstration on optical platform reliably distinguishes between several strategies.
AI.conclusion: Provides a strong and robust tool for causal inference in quantum networks that works without device knowledge and is experimentally viable.

title: Telemetry-Based Server Selection in the Quantum Internet via Cross-Layer Runtime Estimation
summary: The Quantum Internet will allow clients to delegate quantum workloads to remote servers over heterogeneous networks, but choosing the server that minimizes end-to-end execution time is difficult because server processing, feedforward classical communication, and entanglement distribution can overlap in protocol-dependent ways and shift the runtime bottleneck. We propose $T_{\max}$, a lightweight runtime score that sums coarse telemetry from multiple layers to obtain a conservative ranking for online server selection without calibrating weights for each deployment. Using NetSquid discrete-event simulations of a modified parameter-blind VQE (PB-VQE) workload, we evaluate $T_{\max}$ on pools of 10,000 heterogeneous candidates (selecting among up to 100 per decision) across crossover and bottleneck-dominated regimes, including temporal jitter scenarios and jobs with multiple shots. $T_{\max}$ achieves single-digit mean regret normalized by the oracle (below 10%) in both regimes and remains in the single-digit range under classical communication latency jitter for multi-shot jobs, while performance degrades for single-shot jobs under severe jitter. To connect performance to deployment planning, we derive an operating map based on requirements relating distance and entanglement rate requirements to protocol level counts, quantify how simple multiuser contention shifts the crossover, and use Sobol global sensitivity analysis to identify regime-dependent bottlenecks. These findings suggest that simple cross-layer telemetry can enable practical server selection while providing actionable provisioning guidance for emerging Quantum Internet services.

AI.tldr: A lightweight runtime scoring method called T_max for server selection in Quantum Internet that combines cross-layer telemetry to rank servers without weight calibration, achieving low regret in simulations across different network regimes.
AI.motivation: The Quantum Internet will enable delegation of quantum workloads to remote servers, but selecting the optimal server is challenging due to overlapping components (server processing, classical communication, entanglement distribution) that create protocol-dependent bottlenecks and shift runtime constraints.
AI.method: Proposed T_max, a lightweight runtime score that sums coarse telemetry from multiple layers to obtain conservative server rankings without requiring weight calibration for each deployment. Evaluated using NetSquid discrete-event simulations of modified parameter-blind VQE workloads across heterogeneous server pools (10,000 candidates, selecting up to 100 per decision) in crossover and bottleneck-dominated regimes, including temporal jitter scenarios and multi-shot jobs.
AI.result: T_max achieves single-digit mean regret normalized by oracle (below 10%) in both crossover and bottleneck-dominated regimes. Maintains single-digit performance under classical communication latency jitter for multi-shot jobs, though degrades for single-shot jobs under severe jitter. Derived operating maps connecting distance/entanglement rate requirements to protocol counts, quantified multiuser contention effects on crossover points, and used Sobol sensitivity analysis to identify regime-dependent bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Simple cross-layer telemetry can enable practical server selection for Quantum Internet services while providing actionable provisioning guidance. The approach demonstrates that lightweight scoring without complex calibration can achieve near-optimal performance across diverse network conditions and workload types.

title: Restriction-Based Certificate of Bipartite Schmidt Rank in Hypergraph States
summary: We investigate bipartite entanglement in qubit hypergraph states across an arbitrary fixed bipartition. Using the real equally weighted (REW) representation, the Schmidt rank across the cut can be computed as the real rank of a phase-cleaned cross-cut sign matrix. Whereas graph states admit an exact cut-rank rule, because the cross-cut phase is purely bilinear, hypergraph states typically contain higher-degree cross-cut interactions, for which the cut-rank rule fails. Our approach certifies entanglement by fixing a single computational-basis assignment on a subset of qubits, thereby selecting a submatrix on an active slice. When this restriction removes all higher-degree cross-cut residues, the remaining cross-cut phase becomes bilinear up to cut-local terms. We call the resulting submatrices residual-free bilinear cores and show that they yield an exponential Schmidt-rank lower bound in terms of the $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank of an exposed core matrix. We further give a combinatorial sufficient condition, phrased as a disjoint bridge matching, that guarantees the existence of large full-rank cores for broad families of CCZ-type bridge patterns, and we present a search-and-verify procedure that constructs and certifies such cores directly from the hyperedge description.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a method to certify bipartite entanglement in qubit hypergraph states by identifying residual-free bilinear cores that yield exponential Schmidt-rank lower bounds.
AI.motivation: While graph states have exact cut-rank rules due to purely bilinear cross-cut interactions, hypergraph states contain higher-degree cross-cut interactions that break these rules, requiring new methods to certify entanglement across arbitrary bipartitions.
AI.method: Using real equally weighted (REW) representation, the approach fixes computational-basis assignments on qubit subsets to select active slices, removing higher-degree cross-cut residues to obtain residual-free bilinear cores. These cores yield Schmidt-rank lower bounds via F₂-rank of exposed core matrices. A combinatorial condition (disjoint bridge matching) guarantees large full-rank cores for CCZ-type bridge patterns, with a search-and-verify procedure constructing cores directly from hyperedge descriptions.
AI.result: The method provides exponential Schmidt-rank lower bounds for hypergraph states by identifying residual-free bilinear cores. The combinatorial condition ensures existence of large full-rank cores for broad CCZ-type bridge pattern families, enabling entanglement certification.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a framework for certifying bipartite entanglement in hypergraph states through residual-free bilinear cores, overcoming limitations of graph state cut-rank rules and providing constructive methods for entanglement analysis across arbitrary bipartitions.

title: Asynchronous Multi-photon Interference for Quantum Networks
summary: Advanced quantum communication protocols require high-visibility quantum interference between photons generated at distant nodes, which places stringent demands on optical synchronization. Conventionally, synchronization of optical wave packets relies on pulsed sources and precise optical path stabilization. An alternative approach employs continuous-wave (CW) photon-pair sources, where temporal indistinguishability is enforced by post-selecting detection events within a coincidence window $τ_w$ shorter than the photon coherence time $T_c$. Despite its conceptual simplicity, the quantitative relation between relevant time scales, achievable interference visibility, and usable multi-photon rates has remained unclear. Here, we develop in detail and experimentally validate a theoretical framework that quantitatively describes time-resolved multi-photon interference in the CW regime. We explicitly incorporate detector timing jitter, photon coherence time, and temporal post-selection. The model is verified using four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference measurements. Based on this validated framework, we determine the coincidence window that maximizes usable four-photon rates for a target visibility. Finally, we compare CW and pulsed SPDC sources under equivalent indistinguishability constraints and show that CW operation can achieve comparable rates while relaxing optical synchronization requirements.

AI.tldr: Theoretical framework for time-resolved multi-photon interference with continuous-wave photon-pair sources, validated experimentally, showing CW operation can achieve comparable rates to pulsed sources while relaxing synchronization requirements.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication requires high-visibility photon interference, but conventional pulsed sources demand precise optical synchronization. CW sources offer an alternative but lack clear quantitative understanding of how time scales affect interference visibility and usable photon rates.
AI.method: Developed theoretical framework incorporating detector timing jitter, photon coherence time, and temporal post-selection. Validated using four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference measurements. Determined optimal coincidence window for maximizing usable four-photon rates at target visibility.
AI.result: Framework successfully validated experimentally. Showed CW operation can achieve comparable multi-photon rates to pulsed SPDC sources under equivalent indistinguishability constraints while relaxing optical synchronization requirements.
AI.conclusion: CW photon-pair sources provide a viable alternative to pulsed sources for quantum communication, offering comparable performance with reduced synchronization complexity, enabled by proper understanding and optimization of temporal parameters.

title: Correcting coherent quantum errors by going with the flow
summary: The performance of a given quantum error correction (QEC) code depends upon the noise model that is assumed. Independent Pauli noise, applied after each quantum operation, is a simplistic noise model that is easy to simulate and understand in the context of stabilizer codes. Although such a noise model is artificial, it is equivalent to independent, random, unbiased qubit rotations. What about spatially or temporally correlated qubit rotations? Such a noise model is applicable to global operations (e.g., NMR or ESR), common control sources (e.g., lasers), or slow drift (e.g., charge or magnetic noise) in various qubit technologies. In the worst case, such errors can combine constructively and result in a post-correction failure rate that increases with the number of error correction cycles. However, we show that this worst case does not generally arise unless taking active corrective actions while performing QEC. That is, by employing virtual Pauli frame updates ("passive" error correction) rather than physical corrections ("active" error correction), coherent errors do not compound appreciably. Starting in a random Pauli frame is also advantageous. In fact, through perturbation theory arguments and supporting numerical simulations, we show that the logical qubit performance beyond distance 3 for correlated single-qubit Hamiltonian noise models (i.e., global errant qubit rotations), when employing these "lazy" strategies, essentially matches the performance of Pauli noise model with the same process fidelity (fidelity after one application). In a more general circuit model of noise, correlations may add constructively within syndrome extraction rounds but Pauli frame randomization from passive error correction mitigates this effect across multiple rounds.

AI.tldr: Passive error correction with virtual Pauli frame updates and random initial frames mitigates coherent error accumulation from correlated qubit rotations, matching Pauli noise performance beyond distance 3 codes.
AI.motivation: Current quantum error correction analysis often assumes simplistic independent Pauli noise, but realistic noise includes spatially/temporally correlated qubit rotations from global operations, common control sources, or slow drift. These coherent errors can combine constructively across QEC cycles, potentially causing failure rates to increase with cycle count.
AI.method: Employ "passive" error correction using virtual Pauli frame updates instead of physical corrections ("active" error correction). Start with random Pauli frames. Use perturbation theory arguments and numerical simulations to analyze performance under correlated single-qubit Hamiltonian noise models (global errant qubit rotations).
AI.result: With passive strategies, coherent errors do not compound appreciably. Beyond distance 3 codes, logical qubit performance under correlated rotation noise essentially matches Pauli noise performance with the same process fidelity. Pauli frame randomization from passive correction mitigates constructive error correlations across multiple syndrome extraction rounds.
AI.conclusion: Passive error correction with virtual Pauli frame updates and random initialization provides effective mitigation against coherent error accumulation from correlated qubit rotations, making QEC performance comparable to independent Pauli noise models despite more realistic correlated noise.

title: Quantum feedback algorithms for DNA assembly using FALQON variants
summary: Reconstructing DNA sequences without a reference, known as de novo assembly, is a complex computational task involving the alignment of overlapping fragments. To address this problem, a usual strategy is to map the assembly to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation, which can be solved by different quantum algorithms. In this work, we focus on three versions of the Feedback-based Algorithm, a protocol that eliminates classical optimization loops via measurement feedback. We analyze long-read DNA fragments from SARS-CoV-2 and human mitochondrial DNA using standard FALQON, second-order FALQON (SO-FALQON), and time-rescaled FALQON (TR-FALQON). Numerical results show that both variants improve convergence to the ground state and increase success probabilities at reduced circuit depths. These findings indicate that enhanced feedback-driven dynamics are effective for solving combinatorial problems on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Three variants of the Feedback-based Algorithm (FALQON) are applied to de novo DNA assembly via QUBO formulation, showing improved convergence and success probabilities for SARS-CoV-2 and human mitochondrial DNA reconstruction.
AI.motivation: De novo DNA assembly is computationally challenging, and quantum approaches via QUBO formulations offer potential solutions. The study aims to enhance quantum algorithms for this problem by exploring improved feedback-driven dynamics suitable for near-term quantum hardware.
AI.method: The paper applies three versions of the Feedback-based Algorithm (FALQON) to de novo DNA assembly: standard FALQON, second-order FALQON (SO-FALQON), and time-rescaled FALQON (TR-FALQON). These algorithms map DNA assembly to QUBO problems and use measurement feedback to eliminate classical optimization loops. The methods are tested on long-read DNA fragments from SARS-CoV-2 and human mitochondrial DNA.
AI.result: Numerical results demonstrate that both SO-FALQON and TR-FALQON variants improve convergence to the ground state and increase success probabilities compared to standard FALQON, while operating at reduced circuit depths.
AI.conclusion: Enhanced feedback-driven dynamics, as implemented in SO-FALQON and TR-FALQON, are effective for solving combinatorial optimization problems like de novo DNA assembly on near-term quantum hardware, offering improved performance with shallower quantum circuits.

title: On Hydrodynamic Formulations of Quantum Mechanics and the Problem of Sparse Ontology
summary: Hydrodynamic reformulations of the Schrödinger equation suggest an interpretation of quantum mechanics in terms of a fluid flowing on configuration space. In the discrete hydrodynamic view, this fluid is not fundamental but emerges from many underlying microscopic fluid components whose collective behavior reproduces quantum phenomena. The most developed realization of this idea is the discrete many interacting worlds (MIW) framework, in which discrete particle-like worlds interact via inter-world forces and quantum probabilities are grounded in direct world counting. But there is also an older, continuous version of MIW. After reviewing the hydrodynamic and MIW formalisms, and emphasizing some of their interpretational advantages over the Everettian Many Worlds and Bohmian approaches, we argue that all discrete hydrodynamic models face a generic structural difficulty, which we call the problem of sparse ontology. Because wavefunctions typically branch under decoherence, the discrete components of the fluid are repeatedly partitioned into sub-ensembles, thereby thinning their density in configuration space and driving the dynamics away from the quantum regime once the components become sufficiently sparse. We conclude that successful hydrodynamic completions of quantum mechanics plausibly require an essentially continuous ontology.

AI.tldr: Discrete hydrodynamic models of quantum mechanics face a "sparse ontology" problem where wavefunction branching under decoherence thins component density, causing deviation from quantum behavior when components become too sparse.
AI.motivation: To analyze hydrodynamic reformulations of Schrödinger equation that interpret quantum mechanics as emergent fluid dynamics on configuration space, comparing discrete vs. continuous approaches and identifying structural limitations of discrete models.
AI.method: Review hydrodynamic and Many Interacting Worlds (MIW) formalisms, analyze interpretational advantages over Everettian Many Worlds and Bohmian approaches, and examine the structural problem of sparse ontology in discrete hydrodynamic models.
AI.result: Discrete hydrodynamic models face a generic structural difficulty: wavefunction branching under decoherence repeatedly partitions discrete components into sub-ensembles, thinning their density in configuration space and driving dynamics away from quantum regime when components become sufficiently sparse.
AI.conclusion: Successful hydrodynamic completions of quantum mechanics plausibly require an essentially continuous ontology rather than discrete components, due to the fundamental sparse ontology problem in discrete models.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization for Decoding of Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
summary: Decoding Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes is a fundamental problem in coding theory, and Belief Propagation (BP) is one of the most popular methods for LDPC code decoding. However, BP may encounter convergence issues and suboptimal performance, especially for short-length codes and in high-noise channels. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a type of Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) designed to solve combinatorial optimization problems by minimizing a problem-specific cost function. In this paper, we present a QAOA-based decoding framework for LDPC codes by formulating a decoding cost function that incorporates both parity-check constraints and soft channel reliability information. The resulting optimization problem is solved using QAOA to search for low-energy configurations corresponding to valid codewords. We test the proposed method through extensive numerical experiments and compare its performance with BP decoding. The experimental results demonstrate that the QAOA-based decoder achieves a higher probability of correctly recovering the transmitted codeword than BP across multiple experimental settings.

AI.tldr: QAOA-based decoder for LDPC codes outperforms Belief Propagation in error correction performance across multiple experimental settings.
AI.motivation: BP decoding for LDPC codes has convergence issues and suboptimal performance, especially for short-length codes and high-noise channels, motivating exploration of quantum optimization approaches.
AI.method: Formulated a decoding cost function incorporating parity-check constraints and soft channel reliability information, then solved using QAOA to search for low-energy configurations corresponding to valid codewords.
AI.result: QAOA-based decoder achieves higher probability of correctly recovering transmitted codewords than BP across multiple experimental settings.
AI.conclusion: QAOA provides an effective quantum optimization framework for LDPC code decoding that outperforms classical BP methods, demonstrating the potential of quantum algorithms for coding theory problems.

title: Exact quantum transport in non-Markovian open Gaussian systems
summary: We build an exact framework to evaluate heat, energy, and particle transport between Gaussian reservoirs mediated by a quadratic quantum system. By combining full counting statistics with newly developed non-Markovian master equation approaches, we introduce an effective master equation whose solution can be used to generate arbitrary moments of the heat statistics for any number of reservoirs. This theory applies equally to fermionic and bosonic systems, holds at arbitrarily strong coupling, and resolves out-of-equilibrium transient dynamics determined by the system's initial state. In the steady-state, weak-coupling limit, we recover results analogous to those of the well-known Landauer-Büttiker formalism. We conclude our discussion by demonstrating an application of the method to a prototypical fermionic system. Our results uncover a regime of transient negative heat conductance contingent upon the initial system preparation, providing a clear signature of non-trivial out-of-equilibrium dynamics.
